# Why testing your assumptions doesn't protect you {#sec-appendix-assumption-tests}

```{r}
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
library(here)
library(brms)
library(posterior)
library(ggdist)

# The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)
Plot_theme <- source("functions/plot_theme.R")
Plot_theme <- Plot_theme$value

# The histology data, used in the last section
cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))
cell_data$DPI <- as.numeric(cell_data$DPI)
cell_data$DPI_f <- factor(cell_data$DPI)
```

You have read this paragraph, and you may have written it: "Normality was assessed with the Shapiro-Wilk test (p = 0.21) and homogeneity of variances with Levene's test (p = 0.38). Assumptions were met, so we proceeded with the analysis." It sounds like diligence. It has the grammar of a safety inspection. My argument in this appendix is that the second sentence is not something those two numbers can support, and that the habit behind it gives you the feeling of having checked without the substance. I will make that argument the only way I find convincing, which is by building data where we know the truth and watching what the tests do with it. The main text, in @sec-linear-regression-assumptions, makes the case with one real dataset. Here we stress it.

One caution before we start, because the claim is easy to overstate. I am not saying that tests of assumptions are useless for everything. I am saying they are useless for the job people hire them to do, which is to certify that a model is fine. That is a narrower claim, and it is the one the evidence supports.

## What an assumption test is actually asking

A car's check-engine light is wired to specific sensors. It will come on for a loose gas cap, and it will stay dark while the brake pads wear through, because nobody wired a sensor to the brake pads. An assumption test is that light. Shapiro-Wilk is wired to one thing: how far the shape of your residuals sits from a normal distribution. Levene's test is wired to another: whether the spread differs across groups. Neither knows what your scientific claim is, and neither can tell you whether the deviation it detects would change that claim.

Formally, each test takes as its null hypothesis that the assumption holds *exactly*, and returns how surprising your data would be under that null. That is the same smoke alarm as in @sec-appendix-p-values, with the same two limitations. A small p-value says the deviation is detectable, not that it matters. A large p-value says the test did not detect anything, not that nothing is there. Those two sentences are the whole appendix; the rest is evidence.

## The alarm follows your sample size, not the damage

If a test is a good guide to whether an assumption has been violated badly enough to matter, its alarm rate should follow the damage. So let's measure the damage directly. I simulate on purpose here, because it is the only way to know the truth: in real data you never know whether an assumption fails or by how much, but in simulated data you do.

The setup is a straight line with a true slope of 0.5 and errors that are not normal: moderately heavy-tailed (a *t* distribution with 5 degrees of freedom, rescaled to unit variance). That is a deviation from normality that most textbooks, including the ones this book cites, would tell you linear regression tolerates. For each sample size from 10 to 5,000 I generate 1,000 datasets and record two things: whether Shapiro-Wilk raised an alarm on the residuals, and whether the ordinary 95% confidence interval for the slope contained the true value of 0.5. The second is the damage. I call it [coverage]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: the share of intervals that catch the truth, which should be 95%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-appendix_alarm_vs_n
#| fig-cap: Shapiro-Wilk alarm rate and actual coverage of the 95% interval for the slope, as sample size grows. Errors are heavy-tailed (t with 5 df), 1,000 simulated datasets per sample size.
#| fig-alt: Line plot against sample size on a log axis. The alarm rate climbs from about 9 percent at n of 10 to 100 percent from n of 1,000. Coverage of the 95 percent interval stays flat at about 95 percent at every sample size.
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2

# Fixed seed so the simulation is the same on every render
set.seed(101)

# For each sample size: 1,000 datasets with a true slope of 0.5 and heavy-tailed errors
exp1 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(10, 20, 50, 200, 1000, 5000), function(n) {
  x <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = n)
  res <- t(vapply(seq_len(1000), function(i) {
    # t errors with 5 df, rescaled to unit variance
    e <- rt(n, df = 5) / sqrt(5 / 3)
    y <- 1 + 0.5 * x + e
    fit <- lm(y ~ x)
    ci <- confint(fit)[2, ]
    # Did Shapiro-Wilk raise an alarm, and did the interval cover the true slope?
    c(shapiro.test(residuals(fit))$p.value < 0.05, ci[1] <= 0.5 & ci[2] >= 0.5)
  }, numeric(2)))
  data.frame(n = n, alarm = mean(res[, 1]), coverage = mean(res[, 2]))
}))

# Long format: one row per sample size and quantity
exp1_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(n = exp1$n, share = exp1$alarm, what = "Shapiro-Wilk raises an alarm"),
  data.frame(n = exp1$n, share = exp1$coverage, what = "Interval for the slope covers the truth")
)

# Both rates against sample size; direct labels replace the legend
ggplot(exp1_long, aes(x = n, y = share, color = what, shape = what)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10, 20, 50, 200, 1000, 5000), labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Shapiro-Wilk raises an alarm" = "#D55E00",
                                "Interval for the slope covers the truth" = "#0072B2")) +
  annotate("text", x = 12, y = 0.30, label = "Alarm rate", color = "#D55E00", hjust = 0, size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 12, y = 0.88, label = "Coverage (target: 95%)", color = "#0072B2", hjust = 0, size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Sample size (log scale)", y = "Share of simulated datasets") +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_none()
```

I draw this one as two labelled lines from `ggplot2` because the whole argument is a comparison of two curves over the same axis, and labelling the lines directly saves the reader a trip to a legend. At 10 observations (@fig-appendix_alarm_vs_n) the alarm sounds in `r round(100 * exp1$alarm[exp1$n == 10])`% of datasets, barely above the 5% a test raises by luck alone. At 200 it sounds in `r round(100 * exp1$alarm[exp1$n == 200])`%, and from 1,000 on it sounds every time. Over exactly the same range, the interval for the slope does what it is supposed to do: coverage sits between `r round(100 * min(exp1$coverage), 1)`% and `r round(100 * max(exp1$coverage), 1)`% at every sample size. Nothing got worse as the alarm got louder. The test is measuring how well it can see the heavy tails, which depends on how many observations it has, and not how much they hurt the inference. This is the central-limit-theorem argument from the main chapter, seen from the other side: the larger your sample, the less the shape of the residuals matters for the line, and the more eagerly the test objects to it.

## And silent exactly where it hurts

The reverse failure is worse, because it is the one that sends a flawed analysis to a journal with a clean bill of health. Take dependence. Twelve animals, six control and six treated, five measurements per animal, and *no* true treatment effect. Each animal has its own baseline (a random intercept with a standard deviation of 1) and each measurement its own noise (also a standard deviation of 1), so measurements from the same animal are correlated, with a correlation of 0.5. Now do what the rotarod example in the main chapter warned about: ignore the animals and fit `lm(y ~ treatment)` to all 60 rows as if they were independent.

For 1,000 such datasets I record whether the 95% interval for the treatment effect covered the truth (zero), and whether each of five common diagnostics raised an alarm: Shapiro-Wilk on the residuals; the non-constant variance score test from the `car` package; Levene's test across the two groups; and a lag-1 autocorrelation test (the same family of idea as Durbin-Watson) run twice, once with the rows in a shuffled order, the way a spreadsheet might happen to have them, and once with the rows sorted by animal.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-appendix_tests_clustered
#| tbl-cap: How often each diagnostic raised an alarm when 12 animals with 5 measurements each were analyzed as 60 independent rows, with no true effect

# Design: 12 animals, 5 measurements each, no true treatment effect
set.seed(202)

n_animals <- 12
rows_per_animal <- 5

# One simulated dataset, analyzed as if all 60 rows were independent
one_clustered_dataset <- function() {
  animal <- rep(seq_len(n_animals), each = rows_per_animal)
  treat <- as.numeric(animal > n_animals / 2)
  # Animal baseline plus measurement noise, so rows of one animal are correlated
  y <- rnorm(n_animals, 0, 1)[animal] + rnorm(n_animals * rows_per_animal, 0, 1)
  fit <- lm(y ~ treat)
  r <- residuals(fit)
  ci <- confint(fit)["treat", ]
  levene_p <- anova(lm(abs(y - ave(y, treat, FUN = median)) ~ factor(treat)))$`Pr(>F)`[1]
  # Covered the truth, then five diagnostics that may raise an alarm
  out <- c(
    ci[1] <= 0 & ci[2] >= 0,
    shapiro.test(r)$p.value < 0.05,
    car::ncvTest(fit)$p < 0.05,
    levene_p < 0.05,
    Box.test(sample(r), lag = 1, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value < 0.05,
    Box.test(r, lag = 1, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value < 0.05
  )
  names(out) <- c("covered", "shapiro", "ncv", "levene", "lag1_shuffled", "lag1_by_animal")
  out
}

# Average over 1,000 datasets
exp2 <- colMeans(t(vapply(seq_len(1000), function(i) one_clustered_dataset(), numeric(6))))

# Share of datasets flagged by each diagnostic
exp2_tbl <- data.frame(
  check = c("Shapiro-Wilk on the residuals",
            "Non-constant variance score test (car::ncvTest)",
            "Levene's test across the two groups",
            "Lag-1 autocorrelation test, rows in shuffled order",
            "Lag-1 autocorrelation test, rows sorted by animal"),
  flagged = unname(exp2[c("shapiro", "ncv", "levene", "lag1_shuffled", "lag1_by_animal")])
)

gt(exp2_tbl) |>
  cols_label(check = "Diagnostic", flagged = "Datasets flagged") |>
  fmt_percent(columns = flagged, decimals = 0)
```

@tbl-appendix_tests_clustered has the answer. The interval that claims to be 95% covered the truth in `r round(100 * exp2["covered"])`% of these datasets. Put differently, an analysis with a nominal 5% false-positive rate declared an effect that did not exist in about `r round(100 * (1 - exp2["covered"]))`% of them. And the diagnostics? Shapiro-Wilk and the shuffled-rows autocorrelation test sit at about the 5% that luck alone would give. The two variance tests flag a bit more, but for the wrong reason: they notice that the two groups differ in spread, and the cure they point to (an unequal-variance correction) addresses a different problem from the one we have. The single check that finds the damage, the lag-1 test on rows sorted by animal, works only if you already know the animal structure well enough to sort by it.

That is the lesson of this simulation. Independence is a property of how the data were collected, not of what the residuals look like, and no test of the residuals can substitute for knowing your design. When the structure is known, you do not need a test: you model it, which is what @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts is for.

## Test first, then choose

The third failure is a procedure rather than a test. It is the textbook workflow: check an assumption with a test, then use the result to choose the method. Compare two groups; run Levene's test; if it flags unequal variances use Welch's *t*-test, otherwise use Student's. It sounds like prudence. George Box compared the practice of testing variances before a comparison of means to putting to sea in a rowing boat to find out whether the water is calm enough for an ocean liner to leave port [@box1953], and later work has confirmed that such preliminary tests distort the error rates of the analysis that follows [@rochon2012; @harrell2015].

Here is the distortion, in a situation that is common at the bench: a small group (10 animals) and a large one (40), no true difference, and a small group that is more variable than the large one by a ratio that I vary from 1 (equal spread) to 3. For each ratio, 5,000 simulated experiments. I record how often each procedure declares a difference at the 5% level, which should be 5%.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-appendix_two_stage
#| tbl-cap: False-positive rate of three ways to compare two groups when there is no true difference, small group of 10 and large group of 40, 5,000 simulated experiments per row

# A small and a large group with no true difference; the small one is more variable
set.seed(303)

# One experiment: Student, Welch and the Levene-then-choose procedure
one_comparison <- function(ratio) {
  y <- c(rnorm(10, 0, ratio), rnorm(40, 0, 1))
  g <- factor(rep(1:2, c(10, 40)))
  student <- t.test(y ~ g, var.equal = TRUE)
  welch <- t.test(y ~ g)
  levene_p <- anova(lm(abs(y - ave(y, g, FUN = median)) ~ g))$`Pr(>F)`[1]
  chosen <- if (levene_p < 0.05) welch else student
  c(student$p.value < 0.05, welch$p.value < 0.05, chosen$p.value < 0.05, levene_p < 0.05)
}

# 5,000 experiments for each spread ratio
exp3 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 1.5, 2, 3), function(ratio) {
  r <- colMeans(t(vapply(seq_len(5000), function(i) one_comparison(ratio), numeric(4))))
  data.frame(sd_ratio = ratio, student = r[1], welch = r[2], twostage = r[3], levene = r[4])
}))

gt(exp3) |>
  cols_label(sd_ratio = "Spread ratio (small group / large group)",
             student = "Student (equal variances)",
             welch = "Welch (unequal variances)",
             twostage = "Levene first, then choose",
             levene = "Levene raises an alarm") |>
  fmt_number(columns = sd_ratio, decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = -sd_ratio, decimals = 0)
```

Read @tbl-appendix_two_stage row by row. With equal spreads all three procedures behave, and Welch gives up nothing in false positives: it is as good as Student when Student's assumption is true. As the ratio grows, Student's false-positive rate climbs to `r round(100 * exp3$student[exp3$sd_ratio == 3])`%, as expected. Welch holds at about 5% in every row. The two-stage procedure is the interesting column. At a ratio of 2 the pretest catches the problem in only `r round(100 * exp3$levene[exp3$sd_ratio == 2])`% of experiments, so the combined procedure still gives `r round(100 * exp3$twostage[exp3$sd_ratio == 2])`% false positives, nearly double what it advertises. It looks best, at `r round(100 * exp3$twostage[exp3$sd_ratio == 3])`%, in the row where the problem is so blatant (the alarm sounds `r round(100 * exp3$levene[exp3$sd_ratio == 3])`% of the time) that you did not need a test to see it. The pretest protects you when you need it least, and the simplest strategy, using Welch's test always, beats the whole ritual.

## A fair word for the tests

None of this makes every diagnostic worthless. A surprising alarm is a perfectly good reason to go and *look* at a plot, which is the use I would defend. In a pipeline that fits hundreds of models, where nobody can inspect every residual plot, an automated screen that decides which fits get a human look is sensible. And some diagnostics are not tests at all but measurements with an interpretable scale: the ratio of two group spreads, Cook's distance for a single influential animal. What I am arguing against is the pass-fail reading, the sentence "assumptions were met", because that is the one thing a test of the residuals cannot give you. @anscombe1973 made the same point half a century ago with four datasets that share the same summary numbers and the same fitted line and look nothing alike on a page: graphs are essential, and numbers alone can be automated into a false sense of security.

## What to do instead

The books this one leans on are remarkably consistent about the alternative. Gelman, Hill, and Vehtari do not recommend diagnostics of residual normality at all, and rank the assumptions that matter by what they do to your inference, not by what a test can detect [@gelman2020]. The *Bayesian Workflow* authors say that the goal is not to reject null hypotheses, since we know ahead of time that nearly all our models are wrong, but to explore how they fail, with graphs of the data against the fitted model as the most useful tool [@gelman2026]. McElreath asks the same of you: assess exactly how the model fails to describe the data and use your judgment, and that of your colleagues, to decide whether the failure matters [@mcelreath2020]. Kruschke points out that in Bayesian software it is straightforward to relax the usual normal-and-equal-variances assumptions directly [@kruschke2015]. And Inchausti, whose dual approach this book follows, relies on graphical residual diagnostics when he fits his models and skips formal pretests [@inchausti2023]. Turned into a procedure:

1. **Decide which assumptions carry your claim.** For the slope of a line, linearity and a defensible design matter most, and normality barely at all. For a prediction interval for one new animal, the spread and the tails matter much more.
2. **Look, with a picture and a quantity matched to the claim.** Residuals by group, as in the main chapter. Posterior predictive checks of the mean and the standard deviation per day, which ask whether the model can reproduce the feature your question depends on (@sec-mcmc-model-checking).
3. **Relax instead of testing.** Fit the model with the assumption loosened, and see whether the answer you care about moves. If it does not, the assumption was not carrying your claim and you can stop worrying. If it does, report the loosened model.
4. **Say what you did.** Which assumptions you examined, how, what you found and what you changed.

Step 3 is the one that replaces a test, so let's run it on real data. We return to the full-range line for tissue area from @sec-linear-regression-assumptions, and ask a question a reader of that experiment would actually ask: how much does tissue area change between day 7 and day 14? Under a straight line, the answer is seven times the slope. I fit three models. The line with normal errors, as in the main chapter. The same line with Student-t errors, which relaxes normality. And a model in which every day gets its own mean *and* its own spread (`sigma ~ DPI_f`), which relaxes linearity and equal variance at once. I leave the `brms` default priors in all three, as in the main chapter: the point here is to see whether the assumptions move the answer, not to elicit priors.

```{r}
# Straight line with normal errors, the main chapter's model (cached)
assumptions_fit <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ DPI,
  data = cell_data,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/linear-regression-assumptions_fit1.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)

# The same line with Student-t errors: relaxes normality (cached)
student_fit <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ DPI,
  data = cell_data,
  family = student(),
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/appendix-assumption-tests_fit1.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)

# One mean and one spread per day: relaxes linearity and equal variance (cached)
free_fit <- brm(
  bf(Tissue_Area ~ DPI_f, sigma ~ DPI_f),
  data = cell_data,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/appendix-assumption-tests_fit2.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Sampler checks that stop the render if a fit fails them
diag_ok <- function(fit) {
  d <- summarise_draws(as_draws_df(fit), "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")
  n_div <- sum(subset(nuts_params(fit), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)
  stopifnot(max(d$rhat) < 1.01, min(d$ess_bulk) > 400, min(d$ess_tail) > 400, n_div == 0)
  c(rhat = max(d$rhat), ess = min(d$ess_bulk, d$ess_tail), divergent = n_div)
}
diag_all <- rbind(line = diag_ok(assumptions_fit), student = diag_ok(student_fit), free = diag_ok(free_fit))

# Posterior draws and the day 7 to day 14 change under each model
d_line <- as_draws_df(assumptions_fit)
d_student <- as_draws_df(student_fit)
d_free <- as_draws_df(free_fit)

change_line <- 7 * d_line$b_DPI
change_student <- 7 * d_student$b_DPI
change_free <- d_free$b_DPI_f14 - d_free$b_DPI_f7

# 95% interval and median, rounded
qi <- function(x) round(unname(quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))), 1)
q_line <- qi(change_line)
q_student <- qi(change_student)
q_free <- qi(change_free)

# The free model's spread on each day
sigma_draws <- list(
  `0` = exp(d_free$b_sigma_Intercept),
  `3` = exp(d_free$b_sigma_Intercept + d_free$b_sigma_DPI_f3),
  `7` = exp(d_free$b_sigma_Intercept + d_free$b_sigma_DPI_f7),
  `14` = exp(d_free$b_sigma_Intercept + d_free$b_sigma_DPI_f14),
  `30` = exp(d_free$b_sigma_Intercept + d_free$b_sigma_DPI_f30)
)
sigma_med <- sapply(sigma_draws, median)
```

All three fits pass the sampler checks (the largest Rhat across them is `r sprintf("%.3f", max(diag_all[, "rhat"]))`, the smallest effective sample size is `r round(min(diag_all[, "ess"]))`, and there are no divergent transitions). Now the answer to our question, under each model (@fig-appendix_change_7_14). I use a half-eye from `ggdist` because the point is how the whole posterior moves when an assumption is relaxed, and a bar with an asterisk could not show that the intervals do not even overlap.

```{r}
#| label: fig-appendix_change_7_14
#| fig-cap: Posterior distribution of the change in tissue area between day 7 and day 14 under three models. Dots mark the median, thick and thin bars the 50% and 95% credible intervals.
#| fig-alt: Three half-eye plots of the change in tissue area from day 7 to day 14. The two straight-line models, with normal and with Student-t errors, are centered near minus 1.9 square millimeters with narrow intervals. The model with free means and spreads is centered near minus 4.5 with an interval that does not overlap the other two.
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Order and labels of the three models
model_levels <- c("Straight line, normal errors", "Straight line, Student-t errors", "Free mean and spread per day")

# One row per posterior draw per model
change_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(model = model_levels[1], change = change_line),
  data.frame(model = model_levels[2], change = change_student),
  data.frame(model = model_levels[3], change = change_free)
)
change_df$model <- factor(change_df$model, levels = rev(model_levels))

# Half-eye per model with 50% and 95% intervals
ggplot(change_df, aes(x = change, y = model, fill = model)) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.5, 0.95), point_interval = "median_qi") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Straight line, normal errors" = "#0072B2",
                               "Straight line, Student-t errors" = "#56B4E9",
                               "Free mean and spread per day" = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = "Change in tissue area from day 7 to day 14 (mm²)", y = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_none()
```

Two things happened, and a test told us neither. First, relaxing normality did essentially nothing: the Student-t line puts the change at `r q_student[2]` mm² (95% interval `r q_student[1]` to `r q_student[3]`), against `r q_line[2]` (`r q_line[1]` to `r q_line[3]`) for the normal line. Normality was not carrying this claim, exactly as the Shapiro-Wilk result in the main chapter ($p$ = 0.36) happened to suggest, though for reasons that result could not have told us. Second, relaxing linearity and equal variance changed the answer completely: `r q_free[2]` mm² (`r q_free[1]` to `r q_free[3]`), more than twice as much tissue lost, with an interval that does not overlap the line's. The narrow interval of the straight line is not careful. It is confidently wrong, because the line is being asked to describe two stretches of the time course with one slope.

The spread tells the same story. The free model estimates a spread of about `r round(sigma_med["3"], 1)` mm² at day 3 and between `r round(min(sigma_med[c("0", "7", "14", "30")]), 1)` and `r round(max(sigma_med[c("0", "7", "14", "30")]), 1)` mm² on the other days, whereas the straight line reports a single `r round(median(d_line$sigma), 1)`, which is too large for four days and too small for one. That is the picture the residual plots and the posterior predictive checks in the main chapter were pointing at, now expressed as the number the claim depends on.

::: callout-tip
### Frequentist equivalent

The same free model exists on the frequentist side, but not in `parsnip`, which has no engine that models the spread. `glmmTMB` does, through its `dispformula` argument, and it lands on essentially the same change between day 7 and day 14. As with every pair in this book, the two lenses agree when the data carry the estimate; what the Bayesian fit adds here is the full posterior for each day's spread, estimated from as few as 7 animals.

```{r}
library(glmmTMB)

# One mean and one spread per day by maximum likelihood
free_tmb <- glmmTMB(Tissue_Area ~ DPI_f, dispformula = ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data)

# Day-14 minus day-7 mean and its standard error (variance of a difference)
b <- fixef(free_tmb)$cond
V <- vcov(free_tmb)$cond
est <- unname(b["DPI_f14"] - b["DPI_f7"])
se <- sqrt(V["DPI_f14", "DPI_f14"] + V["DPI_f7", "DPI_f7"] - 2 * V["DPI_f14", "DPI_f7"])
round(c(estimate = est, lower = est - 1.96 * se, upper = est + 1.96 * se), 1)
```
:::

## What I would write in a methods section instead

Putting the pieces together, here is a paragraph that says what was done and lets a reader judge it, in place of "assumptions were met":

> I examined residuals by day and posterior predictive checks of the mean and standard deviation of tissue area at each day, which showed that a single straight line was wrong on average at two of five days and that a single residual spread was too large for four days and too small for one. The 7-to-14-day change under the straight line was `r q_line[2]` mm² (95% credible interval `r q_line[1]` to `r q_line[3]`); under a model with a free mean and spread per day it was `r q_free[2]` mm² (`r q_free[1]` to `r q_free[3]`), and I report the latter. Replacing normal errors with Student-t errors changed the straight-line estimate by `r round(abs(median(change_student) - median(change_line)), 2)` mm², so normality was not carrying the result.

That paragraph contains no p-value and no "assumptions were met", and it tells the reader more than any battery of tests could. It also says something the tests can never say: how much the answer depended on each assumption.
